### **Preface to OCP Java SE 21 Developer (Exam 1Z0-** **830)**

_Part I:_ _OCP Java SE 21 Developer_ of this book provides a comprehensive


coverage of _new topics_ that have come into Java 21 since the release of Java


17 and that are relevant for the _Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam_


_(1Z0-830)_ . Primarily three new topics in Java 21 ( _pattern matching for_


_objects_, _sequenced collections_, and _virtual threads_ ) are included in the


objectives for the new exam _._ Apart from that, the objectives for the _Java SE_


_21 Developer Professional Exam_ did not change significantly from the


.
objectives for the _Java SE 17 Developer Exam_


_Part II:_ _OCP Java SE 17 Developer_ of this book provides extensive


coverage for the following Java certifications:


_Oracle Certified Professional: Java SE 17 Developer_, and its required


_Java SE 17 Developer Exam (1Z0-829)_


_Oracle Certified Professional: Java SE 11 Developer,_ and its required


_Java SE 11 Developer Exam (1Z0-819)_


Part I and Part II together provide a comprehensive resource for Java 21


certification:


_Oracle Certified Professional: Java SE 21 Developer,_ and its required


_Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam (1Z0-830)_


In this preface we provide the necessary details on how best to prepare and


pass the _Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam_ using this programmer’s


guide. The syllabus for this exam is defined by a set of _exam objectives_ that


are presented in Appendix A in Part I. The _new_ topics that have been added


to the _Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam_ since Java 17 are covered


in Part I, and Appendix A provides detailed references where the rest of the


topics are covered in _Part II:_ _OCP Java SE 17 Developer._

#### **About Part I: OCP Java SE 21 Developer**


Our approach to writing Part I has not changed from the one we employed


for our previous books, mainly because it has proved successful. The


emphasis remains on analyzing code scenarios, rather than esoteric syntax


of individual language constructs. The exam continues to require actual


experience with the language, not just mere recitation of facts. We still


claim that proficiency in the language is the key to success.


Part I is no different from our previous books in one other important aspect:


It provides a mixture of theory and practice that enables readers to prepare


for the exam.


All elements found in our previous books (e.g., examples, figures, tables,


review questions, mock exam questions) can be found in this one as well.


We continue to use UML ( _Unified Modeling Language_ ) extensively to


illustrate concepts and language constructs, and all numbered examples


continue to be complete Java programs ready for experimentation.


Each topic is explained and discussed thoroughly with examples, and is


backed by review questions to reinforce the concepts. Part I is not biased


toward any particular platform, but provides platform-specific details where


necessary.


Part I is primarily intended for professionals who want to prepare for the


_Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam_, but it is readily accessible to any


programmer who wants to master the new topics. After mastering the


language and the core APIs by working systematically through Part I and


Part II, the reader can confidently sit for the exam.


Part I has a separate appendix (Appendix A) providing all the pertinent


information on preparing for the exam. Since Part I only covers new topics


that are relevant for the Java 21 exam, it should be used with Part II, which


covers the remaining exam topics.


The table of contents; listings of tables, examples, and figures; and a


comprehensive index facilitate locating topics discussed in Part I. Cross

references are provided where necessary to indicate the relationships


between the various features of Java.


Part I:
In particular, we draw attention to the following features of


Chapter Topics


Each chapter starts with a short summary of the topics covered in the


chapter, pointing out the major concepts that are introduced.


Each chapter starts with a short summary of topics that are prerequisites for


the topics covered in the chapter. _Part II:_ _OCP Java SE 17 Developer_


readily provides coverage for these prerequisites.


_**Exam Objectives**_










[0.2] The number in front of the objective identifies the exam


objective, as defined by Oracle. The objectives are organized


into major sections, detailing the curriculum for the exam.




**Review Questions**


Review questions are provided after every major topic to test and reinforce


the material. The review questions predominantly reflect the kind of


multiple-choice questions that can be asked on the actual exam. On the


exam, the exact number of answers to choose for each question is explicitly


stated. The review questions in Part I follow that practice.


Many questions on the actual exam contain code snippets with line numbers


to indicate that complete implementation is not provided, and that the


necessary missing code to compile and run the code snippets can be


assumed. The review questions in Part I provide complete code


implementations where possible, so that the code can be readily compiled


and run.


Annotated answers to the review questions are provided in Appendix B in


Part I.


**Example 0.1** _Example Source Code_

the material in the book. The source code for the examples can be


downloaded from the website for Part I (see p. xviii), and readily imported

# **1**
### **Pattern Matching for Java Objects**

Chapter Topics


Using _type patterns_ with the `instanceof` _pattern match operator_ and


the _enhanced_ `switch` _construct_ to _type check objects_ .


Using _record patterns_ with the `instanceof` _pattern match operator_


and the _enhanced_ `switch` _construct_ to _deconstruct records_ .


_Type checking_ objects using the `instanceof` _type comparison_


.
_operator_


Writing multi-way branching code using the _traditional_ `switch`


_statement_ and the _traditional_ `switch` _expression_ that allow _constant_


_expressions_ as `case` labels (collectively called the _traditional_ `switch`


_construct_ as opposed to the _enhanced_ `switch` construct that allows


pattern matching).


**Java SE 21 Developer Professional Exam**


**Objectives**


[3.5] Implement inheritance, including


abstract and sealed types as well as record


classes. Override methods, including that


of the Object class. Implement


polymorphism and differentiate between


object type and reference type. Perform


reference type casting, identify object types


using the instanceof operator, and pattern


matching with the instanceof operator and


the switch construct.



_Only pattern matching_


_using the_


`instanceof` _pattern_


_match operator and the_


_enhanced_ `switch`


_construct is covered in_


_this chapter._



Pattern matching allows testing of an object in order to extract data from the


object if it matches a pattern. Although conditional extraction of data from


an object has always been possible, using pattern matching results in code


that is concise, safe, secure, and easier to read and maintain.


We take a deep dive into pattern matching for objects in Java 21 by


exploring the following features of the language:


Using _type patterns_ with the `instanceof` _pattern match operator_


( _finalized in Java 16)_


Using _type patterns_ with the _enhanced_ `switch` _construct_ ( _finalized in_


_Java 21_ )


Using _record patterns_ with the `instanceof` _pattern match operator_


( _finalized in Java 21_ )


Using _record patterns_ with the _enhanced_ `switch` _construct_ ( _finalized_


_in Java 21_ )


Along the way we use relevant code examples to illustrate pattern matching


for objects and identify coding idioms that utilize patterns.

#### 1.1 Type Pattern Matching with the instanceof  Pattern **Match Operator**


The topic in this section may already be familiar, as it was made permanent


in the language back in Java 16. However, it is included here in order to


provide a comprehensive coverage of pattern matching for Java objects in


one place.


**The** `instanceof` **Type Comparison Operator**


The binary `instanceof` operator can be used in two ways: as a _type_


and as a .
_comparison operator_ _pattern match operator_


The `instanceof` _type comparison operator_ has the following syntax for


comparing types:


_reference_expression_ `instanceof` _destination_type_


At runtime, the `instanceof` type comparison operator returns `true` if


the left-hand operand (i.e., the reference value that results from the


evaluation of _reference_expression_ ) can be a _subtype_ of the right-hand


operand ( _destination_type_ ). It always returns `false` if the left-hand


operand is `null` . If the `instanceof` operator returns `true`, the


corresponding type cast expression `(` _destination_type_ `)` when applied to


the left-hand operand _reference_expression_ is guaranteed to be safe:


`(` _destination_type_ `)` _reference_expression_


The compiler only flags a compile-time error if it can conclusively


determine that there can be no common subtype objects between the type of


the _reference_expression_ and the _destination_type_ . A runtime check is


necessary to determine whether the subtype relationship exists as mentioned


earlier. If there is no such relationship between the types, then the cast


`(` _destination_type_ `)` _reference_expression_ will be invalid, resulting in a


We assume the following type declarations in the discussion below.


Click here to view code image

```
 interface IShape {}

 sealed interface IPolygon extends IShape permits Tria

 final class Triangle implements IPolygon {}

```

```
 class Circle implements IShape {}

```

Figure 1.1 shows the inheritance hierarchy for the types. The


implementation of the types is kept simple for illustrative purposes.


**Figure 1.1** _Inheritance Hierarchy_


The _subtype-and-cast_ idiom is commonly used to elicit subtype-specific


behavior of an object referenced by a supertype reference. If the


`instanceof` type comparison operator at (1a) returns `true`, the cast at


(1b) can be safely applied and subtype-specific behavior can be elicited at


(1c).


Click here to view code image


```
 IShape ishape = new Triangle(); // Supertype referenc

 // Using the instanceof type comparison operator. (1)

 if (ishape instanceof Triangle) {      // (1a) C

 Triangle triangle = (Triangle) ishape;  // (1b) C

 System.out.println(triangle);       // (1c) C

 }

```

**The** `instanceof` **Pattern Match Operator**


Figure 1.2 shows the syntax of the `instanceof` operator when used as a


_pattern match operator_ : The `instanceof` pattern match operator


augments the syntax of the `instanceof` type comparison operator with a


_pattern variable_ . The _type pattern_ comprises a _local reference variable_


_declaration_ that is declared with a _destination type_ and a single _pattern_


_variable_ . The `instanceof` pattern match operator essentially combines


the `instanceof` type comparison operator with an implicit type cast and


initialization of the .
_pattern variable_


**Figure 1.2** _The_ `instanceof` _Pattern Match Operator_


At runtime, if the reference value of the object resulting from the evaluation


of the _reference expression_ can be _cast_ to the _destination type_ (i.e., the


_dynamic type_ of the resulting object is a _subtype_ of the _destination type_ ), the


object is said to _match_ the _type pattern_ . Only in this case does the


`instanceof` pattern match operator return `true` and, as a side effect,


_the reference value of the object is cast to the destination type and assigned_


_to the pattern variable_ . The _pattern variable_ is never created or initialized if


the `instanceof` pattern match operator returns `false` . It always returns


`false` if the _reference expression_ is `null` .


The _subtype-and-cast idiom_ can be expressed more compactly with the


`instanceof` pattern match operator as it type checks the object and casts


its reference value that is assigned to the pattern variable, as illustrated


below at (2).


Click here to view code image

```
 IShape ishape = new Triangle(); // Supertype referenc

 // Using the instanceof pattern match operator. (2)

 if (ishape instanceof Triangle triangle) {    // T

 System.out.println(triangle);

 }

```

When the `instanceof` pattern match operator returns `true`, it is said to


_introduce_ a _pattern variable_ into a well-defined scope, which in this case is


the `if` block. The code above at (2) illustrates the case where the static


_narrower_
type of the _reference expression_ ( `IShape` ) is cast to a


_destination type_ ( `Triangle` ). Generally, a runtime check is required in


such cases to ensure that the _dynamic type_ of the _reference expression_ is


assignment compatible to the type of the pattern variable.


The code below illustrates the case where the static type of the reference


expression ( `Triangle` ) is implicitly cast to a _broader destination type_


( `IShape` ), where `IShape` is a supertype of `Triangle` . If the compiler


can determine that a broader cast is required, then the runtime checks for


assignment compatibility of the dynamic type of the reference expression to


the type of the pattern variable is avoided, as broader reference casts are


safe.


Click here to view code image

```
 Triangle triangle = new Triangle();

 if (triangle instanceof IShape ishape) { // IShape i

 System.out.println(ishape);

 }

```

**Valid Operand Types in the** `instanceof` **Pattern Match Operator**


The types of the operands in the `instanceof` pattern match operator can


be _unrelated_, unless the compiler determines that they are _inconvertible_


(i.e., no object of one can be an object of the other type) or will result in an


_unsafe cast_ (i.e., compromise type safety).


We assume the following bare-bones type declarations in the discussion


below:


Click here to view code image

```
 interface Chart {}

 class PieChart implements Chart {}        // N

 final class Flowchart implements Chart {}    // F

```

**Same Types as Operands**


The operands of the `instanceof` pattern match operator can be of the


same type, as shown at (1). This is equivalent to applying an _identity cast_ to


the object denoted by the reference `c` and assigning it to the pattern


variable `cc` .


Click here to view code image




**Unrelated Types as Operands**


In the following method, although the `IShape` interface and the


`PieChart` class are unrelated, they are allowed as operand types in the


`instanceof` pattern match operator at (1).


Click here to view code image

```
 static void unrelatedTypes(IShape s) {

 if (s instanceof PieChart p) {       // (1) U

 System.out.println(p);

 } else {

 System.out.println("Not a PieChart");

 }

 }

```

The method above will always print `Not a PieChart` when the


parameter is a polygon referenced by `IShape` . Since the class `PieChart`


is not `final`, a subclass can extend this class and also implement the


`IShape` interface, as shown below. Such a subclass is both a `PieChart`


and an `IShape` . At runtime, if the parameter referenced by `IShape` is an


object of this subclass, the call to the method above would print the name of


this class.


Click here to view code image


```
 class ExplodedPieChart extends PieChart implements IS

```

Although the compiler will allow operands of unrelated types, it will flag an


error if it can be determined that the types of the operands cannot have any


values (except `null` ) in common (i.e., are inconvertible). Such types are


known as .
_disjoint types_


**Unrelated Classes as Operands**


Classes that are unrelated by inheritance are disjoint classes. Since a class


can only extend one superclass, such disjoint classes cannot be extended to


have any common subclasses. In the code below, the classes `Circle` and


`PieChart` are unrelated by inheritance and their references inconvertible,


resulting in a compile-time error at (1).


Click here to view code image

```
 Circle c = new Circle();

A pattern variable _cannot_ shadow another local variable by the same name

As we have seen, a pattern variable is analogous to a local variable, except


that a local variable has block scope whereas a pattern variable has flow


sensitive scope as explained next.


**Flow Sensitive Scope of Pattern Variables**


The scope of a pattern variable is the places in the code where the program


control can reach only as a consequence of the `instanceof` pattern


match operator returning `true` .


We first examine the scope of a pattern variable in an `if-else` statement.


If the `instanceof` pattern match operator returns `true` in the


conditional of an `if` statement, the pattern variable is introduced and its


scope is the `if` block, as execution would continue in the `if` block. Not


surprisingly, this is also the case for the `if-else` statement. In the code


below, the pattern variable is _not_ accessible in the `else` block when the


`instanceof` pattern match operator returns `true`, since the `else`


block would never be executed.


Click here to view code image

 System.out.println(triangle);       // Compi

 }

operator introduces a pattern variable if and only if it returns `true` . In the


`if-else` statement below, the `if` block is only executed if the


conditional is `true` —that is, if the `instanceof` pattern match operator


returns `false` . In that case, no pattern variable is introduced, and thus no


pattern variable is ever accessible in the `if` block. However, if the


conditional is `false`, the `instanceof` pattern match operator must be


`true`, and thus introduces a pattern variable that is guaranteed to be


accessible in the `else` block.

 System.out.println(triangle);        // Comp

 } else {

 }

```

and in code after the `if-else` statement.

conditional. The pattern variable will be in scope in the `if` block if the

The conditional- OR operator ( `||` ) does _not_ introduce a pattern variable in

The `instanceof` pattern match operator can also introduce a pattern

and `while` loops. This allows conditional processing of objects where

Using the `instanceof` pattern match operator makes the code more

#### 1.2 Type Pattern Matching with the Enhanced switch **Construct**

The `switch` construct implements a _multi-way branch_ that allows


program control to be transferred to a specific entry point in the code of the


`switch` block based on a selector expression. Java has two variants of the


`switch` construct: the `switch` _statement_ and the `switch` _expression_ .


Each of them can be written in two different ways: Using the _colon_ ( `:` )


_notation_ and the _arrow_ ( `->` ) _notation_ .


Traditionally, only _constant expressions_ were allowed as `case` constants


in the `case` labels of a `switch` construct. The `case` constants could


only be of the following types: Integral types (except `long` ), their


corresponding wrapper types, enum types, or `String` . The code to


execute in the `switch` block is chosen based on an _equality test_ on the


value of the selector expression and the `case` constants in the order of


their specification. We will use the term _traditional_ `switch` _construct_ to


mean `switch` statements and `switch` expressions that have constant


expressions in their `case` labels. Note that there are four ways of writing a


traditional `switch` construct, as the `switch` statement and the `switch`


expression can each be written using the colon notation and the arrow


notation.


The `switch` construct has been enhanced to allow _patterns_ in the `case`


labels of a `switch` construct. The _enhanced_ `switch` _construct_ allows


the value of the selector expression to be matched against patterns in the


`case` labels, and the code associated with the `case` label whose pattern


matches the selector expression is executed. Again, note that there are four


ways of writing the enhanced `switch` construct.


A summary of the `switch` construct is shown in Table 1.1, that applies to


both the traditional and the enhanced `switch` construct. Table 1.2


summarizes how compile-time check for _exhaustiveness_ (i.e., for all


possible values of the selector expression, there must be a matching `case`


label) and _fall-through_ (i.e., whether execution can continue with the code


associated with subsequent `case` labels) are handled in the traditional


`switch` construct. We assume familiarity with the four variations of the


traditional `switch` construct that allows constant expressions in `case`


labels. Our focus here will be on the enhanced `switch` construct that


allows patterns in `case` labels.

**Using Type Patterns in** `case` **Labels**


In an enhanced `switch` construct, the _selector expression_ can be of _any_


_reference type_ and a `case` label can specify a _pattern_ . Such a `case` label


is known as a _pattern label_ and the pattern specified in the `case` label is


called a `case` _pattern_ . The `case` pattern must be _compatible_ with the


selector expression.


If the pattern specified in the `case` label is a _type pattern_, it is called an


_unguarded_ `case` _pattern_ or an _unconditional_ `case` _pattern_, as opposed to


a _guarded_ `case` _pattern_ or a _conditional_ `case` _pattern_ (p. 16). We first


look at specifying unguarded type patterns in `case` labels.


The code below uses the `instanceof` pattern match operator as


conditionals in a cascade `if` - `else` statement to compute the text


representation of certain types of objects, where the reference `obj` of type


`Object` denotes the object.

 result = str.toUpperCase();

 } else if (obj instanceof Point pnt) {

 result = pnt.toString();

 } else if (obj instanceof int[] ia) {

 result = "No match found.";

 }

```

construct. Apart from the `case` label with the `null` value and the


`default` label, all other `case` labels specify type patterns.

The execution of the enhanced `switch` statement proceeds as follows:


The selector expression is evaluated first, resulting in a reference to an


object.


If the selector expression evaluates to `null` and no `case` label with


the `null` value is specified, a `NullPointerException` is thrown.


The selector object is successively matched with the patterns in the


`case` labels.


As we would expect, control is transferred to the start of the code


associated with the first `case` label whose pattern matches the selector


object.


The selector object trivially matches the `default` label if the


`default` label is specified and no matches are found.


An enhanced `switch` construct is always _exhaustive_ —that is, the _type_


_coverage_ of all switch labels (i.e., either a `case` label or the `default`


label) must include the type of the selector expression. The enhanced


`switch` construct guarantees that at least one `case` label or the


`default` label will match the selector object.


If the selector object matches the pattern in a `case` label, any pattern


variables specified in the `case` pattern are introduced into this `case`


label and its associated code. A type pattern introduces a single pattern


variable. Later we will see that a _record pattern_ can introduce more than


.
one pattern variable (p. 20)


Scope of the pattern variables introduced by a pattern is _flow sensitive_ (p.


18 .
)

constant so that appropriate action can be taken if the selector expression

treated as if it has such a `case` label whose associated code throws a

```

 ...

 case null -> throw new NullPointerException(); //

 };

```

A `case` label with the `null` value can occur in any order among the


other switch labels. It can be combined with the `default` label, but not


vice versa, as shown at (1) and (2). If such a combined label is specified, it


must occur last, but then the `case` label with the `null` value or the


`default` label cannot be used individually in the same `switch`


construct, as shown at (3) and (4).

 case default, null -> throw new NullPointerException(

**Guarded Case Patterns**


_clause_ . The code below determines whether an integer is an even or an odd


number. A guarded case pattern is specified in (1) using a `when` clause


`boolean` `ii % 2 == 0` .

Click here to view code image

 case Integer ii when ii % 2 == 0 -> "Even number: "

A `case` label is selected for execution if the selector object matches the


pattern in the `case` label _and_ the associated `when` clause evaluates to


`true` . In the code above, if the `case` label at (1) is not selected, the


unguarded pattern at (2) will always be selected.


The scope of any pattern variable introduced by the pattern comprises the


`when` clause and the code associated with the `case` label. It is a compile

time error if a `when` clause has a constant expression with the value


`false`, as such a `case` label would never be selected.


Any variable that is used but not declared in a `when` clause must be either


`final` or _effectively_ `final` .


A guarded case pattern in the enhanced `switch` construct is equivalent to


a conditional where the operands of the conditional-AND operator ( `&&` )


are a pattern in the `instanceof` pattern match operator and a `boolean`


expression.

**Case Label Dominance**


In a traditional `switch` statement at the most one `case` label can apply,


since the selection of a switch label is based on the equality test. In an


enhanced `switch` statement, several pattern labels can apply, as the value


of the selector expression can be matched by several pattern labels.


Java uses the following heuristic to select a switch label: the first `case`


label in the switch block that matches the selector expression is chosen.


However, this requires _dominance analysis_, analogous to the `catch`


blocks in a `try` - `catch` - `finally` construct. A pattern label results in a


compile-time error if any previous pattern label or constant label _always_


matches first—the former `case` label is said to _dominate_ the latter.


In the code below, (2) will never be executed (i.e., it is _unreachable_ code),


as (1) will always be selected when the number is an `Integer` .


Click here to view code image

```
 Integer num = 1949;

 // Compile-time error: Wrong dominance order for case

 String result2 = switch (num) {

 case Integer ii         -> "Odd number: "

 case Integer ii when ii % 2 == 0 -> "Even number: "

 };

```

The order of the `case` labels shown below will satisfy the dominance


requirement in a `switch` block. In fact, the order in which any constant


`case` label or guarded pattern `case` label is specified is irrelevant, as


long as they are specified _before_ any unguarded pattern `case` labels.


Unguarded pattern `case` labels (e.g., `case Integer ii -> ..` .)


In the code below, the switch expression is exhaustive. The `case` labels


cover all values of the selector expression. Note that a constant `case` label


at (3) is specified after a guarded pattern `case` label at (2), but this is


allowed as mentioned above. However, the two constant `case` labels and


the guarded pattern `case` label are all specified before the unguarded


pattern `case` label at (4). Note that the constant `case` label at (3) will


never be executed.


Click here to view code image

```

 String result = switch (num) {

 case 0        -> "Number is 0";     //

 case Integer ii

 when ii % 2 == 0 -> "Even number: " + ii; //

 case 10        -> "Number is 10";    //

```

```
 case Integer ii    -> "Odd number: " + ii;  //

 };

 System.out.println(result);            //

```

The code above also illustrates that constant `case` labels and pattern


`case` labels can be specified in the same `switch` construct.


Note the special case of a `when` clause whose constant expression


evaluates to `true` . The `case` label at (5) will never be selected, as (4)


(4). Either (4) or (5) has to be omitted for the code to compile.

**Flow Sensitive Scope of a Pattern Variable in** `switch` **Construct**


Analogous to the flow sensitive scope of pattern variables introduced by an


`instanceof` pattern match operator, the scope of a pattern variable


introduced by a `case` label in an enhanced `switch` construct is the


places in the code where the program control can reach only as a


consequence of the `case` pattern matching the selector object. We


summarize the scope of a pattern variable in a `case` label of the enhanced


`switch` construct that can include the following code:


The guard in the `when` clause of a guarded `case` label


The action associated with a switch rule


The statements associated with the `case` label of an enhanced


`switch` statement


**Exhaustiveness of Case Pattern Labels**


Only the _traditional_ `switch` _expression_ with _constant expressions_ in


`case` labels requires that the `switch` block covers all possible values of


_exhaustive_ .

the selector expression—that is, it must be


In contrast, the enhanced `switch` construct (both statement and


expression) requires that the `switch` block is always exhaustive—that is,


the _type coverage_ of its switch labels is exhaustive. Type coverage is the


union of types in the switch labels, and must include the type of the selector


expression. In the code below, the union of types in the switch labels is


`{Integer}` if no `default` label is specified, resulting in a compile-time


error as the type of the selector expression `Number` is not covered by the


union of the label types. Specifying a `default` label makes the `switch`


block exhaustive, since the `default` label covers all types.


Click here to view code image

```
 Number num = 1949;       // Superclass referenc

 String result4 = switch (num) {

 case Integer ii when ii % 2 == 0 -> "Even number: "

 case Integer ii         -> "Odd number: "

 default       -> "Not an Integer"; // (3) Co

 };

```

It should be noted that, if a `default` label is specified, it can occur in _any_


_order_ among the switch labels specified in traditional `switch` construct


(even first), but it is always specified _last_ in enhanced `switch` construct.


A `switch` block _cannot_ have more than one _match-all_ switch label—that


is, _either_ the `default` label _or_ an unguarded pattern `case` label that


matches the selector expression. In the code below, if the `default` label


at (2) is allowed, the `switch` statement will have a second match-all label


in addition to the match-all `case` label at (1) that matches all strings.


Either (1) or (2) is allowed, but not both.


Click here to view code image


```
 static void translateResponse(String response) {

 switch (response.toUpperCase()) {

 case null    -> System.out.println("No respons

 case "NEI"   -> System.out.println("Response i

 case "JA"    -> System.out.println("Response i

 case String s  -> System.out.println("Huh?");

 // default     -> System.out.println("What?");

 }

 }

```

Temptation to make the `switch` construct exhaustive by including a


`default` label should be avoided. Best practice recommends that if


possible, prefer an exhaustive `switch` construct that is without a match

all label.


**Sealed Types and Exhaustiveness**


Permitted types of a sealed type are taken into consideration to ensure


exhaustiveness in an enhanced `switch` construct. The `switch` statement


at (1) is exhaustive in the code below, as the `case` labels cover the


inheritance hierarchy of the sealed type `BankCard` that is the type of the


selector expression. The `default` label is allowed but redundant in this


case. Omitting (2) or (3) will result in a compile-time error.


Click here to view code image


```
 // A sealed type:

 sealed interface BankCard permits DebitCard, CreditCa

 final class DebitCard implements BankCard {}

 final class CreditCard implements BankCard {}

 static void whichCard(BankCard bc) {

 switch (bc) {

 case null      -> System.out.println("No ban

 case DebitCard  dc -> System.out.println("It is

 case CreditCard cc -> System.out.println("It is

 // default -> System.out.println("Huh?");     /

 }

 }

```

**Illegal Fall-Through to a Pattern in** `switch` **Statement**


No fall-through can occur in a `switch` construct that uses the arrow ( `->` )


notation, as the action associated with a switch rule terminates the


execution of the `switch` construct. However, in an enhanced `switch`


construct that uses the colon ( `:` ) notation, a fall-through to a `case` label


that introduces pattern variables is flagged as a compile-time error.


Click here to view code image

```
 Object obj = "Hello";

 switch (obj) {

```

```
 case null   : System.out.println("No string foun

 case String str: System.out.println(str.toUpperCase

 case Point pnt: System.out.println(pnt.toString())

 default    : System.out.println("Unexpected val

 }

```

Referring to line numbers in the code above:


(3) will not have been initialized.


3. If the `break` statement is omitted, execution will continue with the


code associated with the `default` label in (4). This is _legal_ fall

through and is flagged as a compile-time error, as the `default` label


never introduces any pattern variables. One should be wary of such fall

through, as it may introduce logical errors.


Even though the fall-through to the `default` label is allowed in this


particular case, the pattern variable `pnt` cannot be accessed in the code


associated with the `default` label—the scope of the pattern variable


`pnt` excludes the `default` label.


The enhanced `switch` construct does not allow multiple patterns in a


`case` label:


Click here to view code image

```
 case Integer ii, String str -> ...        // C

```

Also, multiple `case` labels are not allowed in a switch label of the


enhanced `switch` construct:


Click here to view code image

```
 case Integer ii, case String str -> ...    // Co

```

However, a _list_ of comma-separated _constant expressions_ is allowed in a


`case` label, regardless of which notation is used.

#### **1.3 Record Patterns**

In addition to using type patterns for pattern matching of objects, we can


also use _record patterns_ that facilitate conditional extraction of component


_record deconstruction_ .

A record pattern specifies _the record type_ and _an optional list of patterns_ in


which each pattern can be _a type pattern_ or _a record pattern_ . In other


words, record patterns can be nested to match the component hierarchy of


nested records. A record pattern allows a record to be matched against a


record type and binds pattern variables in its pattern list to the components


of the record, if a match is found. The list of patterns must match with the


list of components in the record type.


area code, and the local number components by calling the corresponding


accessor methods in the record, respectively. The pattern variables


introduced are then accessible in the `if` block.


Click here to view code image

```
 record PhoneNumber(int countryCode, int areaCode, int

 ...

 Object obj = new PhoneNumber(1, 800, 1234567);

 if (obj instanceof PhoneNumber(int cc, int ac, int ln

```

```

 }

```

The pattern list in the record pattern `PhoneNumber(int cc,` int ac, `int`


`ln)` at (2) consists of three _nested type patterns:_ `int cc`, `int ac`, and


`int ln` . The names of the pattern variables need not be the same as the


component names in the record declaration. Note also that the destination


the destination type of a _top-level type pattern,_ that must always be a


.
_reference type_


A record pattern can be used in contexts where a top-level type pattern can


be used, for example, as an operand of the `instanceof` pattern match


operator (p. 22) and in the `case` labels of an enhanced `switch` construct


.
(p. 26)


An enhanced `for(:)` loop requires a _local variable declaration_ of a loop


variable in its header to successively denote the elements to iterate over. A


record pattern is _not_ a local variable declaration, and therefore cannot be


specified in the header of an enhanced `for(:)` loop, as shown at (1).


However, the local variable declaration in the header of the enhanced


`for(:)` loop at (2) may be considered a top-level _type pattern_, as a type


pattern is syntactically equivalent to a local variable declaration.


Click here to view code image


```
 record Item(int value) {}

 Item[] items = {new Item(10), new Item(20), new Item(

 for (Item(int v) : items) {        // (1) Rec

 System.out.println(v);

 }

 Integer[] intArray = {10, 20, 30, 40};

 for (Integer n : intArray) {        // (2) Loc

 System.out.println(n);

 }

```

As expected, the `null` value does not match any record pattern. If pattern


matching completes abruptly—for example, when an assessor method


throws an exception—a `MatchException` is thrown to indicate an


.

Example 1.1 illustrates using record patterns with the `instanceof`

the code at (1). Using a record pattern to deconstruct a record makes the


code more concise and safer, as the pattern variables in the record pattern


refer to the component values, as illustrated by the code at (2).

 System.out.printf("%d-%d-%d%n", cc, ac, ln);

System.out.printf("%d-%d-%d%n", cc, ac, ln);

Type inference of pattern variables in record patterns can be performed


using `var` —that is, the type of the corresponding component in the record


need not be specified for a type pattern in a record pattern. The code at (3)

variables, where the type of the pattern variables is inferred to be `int` .


**Flow Sensitive Scope of Pattern Variables in Record Patterns**


The flow sensitive scope of the pattern variables in a record pattern is


analogous to that of the pattern variable in a type pattern.


An example of such scope is shown at (4) in Example 1.1, where the pattern


variables are only accessible in the second operand of the conditional- AND


(&&) operator in the `if` conditional and the `if` block, if the


`instanceof` pattern match operator returns `true` .


**Nested Record Patterns**


As record patterns can be nested, they facilitate data navigation of the


component hierarchy of nested records, which are matched recursively. The


nested record class `Contract` at (1) has a record ( `PhoneNumber` ) as a


component. The nested record pattern at (2) allows the component


hierarchy of a `Contact` record to be deconstructed without resorting to


assessor methods.

 ...

 if (obj instanceof

 System.out.printf("%s: %d-%d-%d%n", name, cc, ac, l

 }

```

We can of course make use of type inference of pattern variables using


`var` in nested record patterns, as in (2a), instead of explicitly specifying


the destination type of each type pattern in the pattern list:

```

 Contact(var name, PhoneNumber(var cc, var ac,

 System.out.printf("%s: %d-%d-%d%n", name, cc, ac, l

 }

**Using Record Patterns with Generic Types**


We can specify record patterns for generic record types. Below at (1) is a


declaration of a generic record type, `Pair<T>`, whose two components are


of the same type parameter `T` . A record of this type, parameterized with the


type argument `String`, is constructed at (2).


In a record pattern, the generic record type can be specified with or without


the type arguments. In the latter case, the record type is inferred. The


generic record pattern in (3) is explicitly parameterized with the type


argument `String`, whereas in (4) and (5) the record type is the unbounded


record type `Pair<?>` and the raw record type `Pair`, respectively. The


pattern variable types in (4) and (5) are inferred to be of type `String`


from the record reference `strPair` in the `instanceof` pattern match


operator. In fact, any record of type `Pair<T>` will match the record


patterns in (4) and (5), where the types of the pattern variables is inferred


from the record resulting from the evaluation of the reference expression.


Click here to view code image


```
 record Pair<T>(T item1, T item2) {}

 ...

 Pair<String> strPair = new Pair<>("Milk", "Honey");

 // With parameterization.

 if (strPair instanceof Pair<String>(String a1, String

 System.out.println("Pair1: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 // With unbounded wildcard and using var.

 if (strPair instanceof Pair<?>(var a1, var a2)) {

 System.out.println("Pair2: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 // Without parameterization and using var.

 if (strPair instanceof Pair(var a1, var a2)) {

 System.out.println("Pair3: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 // Diamond operator:

 if (strPair instanceof Pair<>(var a1, var a2)) {

 System.out.println("Pair4: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

```

Parameterizing the record type with the diamond ( `<>` ) operator results in a


compile-time error, as shown above at (6). This operator is used in the


context of calling a constructor and not in record patterns.


Whereas a generic record type can either be explicitly specified with type


arguments or implicitly inferred when omitted in a record pattern, this is not


the case for a generic type pattern. In a generic type pattern, the explicit


type arguments are allowed, and if omitted, are not inferred but treated as


.

**Nested Record Patterns in** `case` **Labels**


Analogous to nested record patterns in the `instanceof` pattern match


operator (p. 23), such patterns can also be specified in the `case` labels of


an enhanced `switch` construct. The nested record class `Contract` at (1)


has a record ( `PhoneNumber` ) as a component. The nested record pattern at


(2) deconstructs the component hierarchy of a `Contact` record safely and


concisely.


Click here to view code image

```
 record Contact(String name, PhoneNumber phoneNumber)

 ...

 Object obj = new Contact("Java Guru", new PhoneNumber

 switch (obj) {

 case Contact(String name, PhoneNumber(int cc, int a

 System.out.printf("%s: %d-%d-%d%n", name, cc, ac,

 }

 default -> System.out.println("No match found.");

 }

```

**Guarded Record Patterns in** `case` **Labels**


Analogous to guarded type patterns in `case` labels (p. 16), record patterns


in an enhanced `switch` construct can be refined using the optional `when`


clause. A `case` label is selected for execution if the selector object


matches the record pattern in the `case` label _and_ the associated `when`


clause evaluates to `true` . Such a guarded case record pattern is used at (1)


below to select any 800 phone numbers. If the `case` label at (1) is not


selected, the unguarded pattern at (2) will always be selected.


Click here to view code image

```
 PhoneNumber pn = new PhoneNumber(1, 800, 5551038);

 switch (pn) {

 case null -> System.out.printf("No phone number fou

 case PhoneNumber(var cc, var ac, var ln) when ac ==

 System.out.println("800 phone numbers cannot be l

 }

 case PhoneNumber(var cc, var ac, var ln) -> {

 String pnToString = String.format("%d-%d-%d", cc,

 System.out.printf("Phone number: %s%n", pnToStrin

 }

 }

```

**Flow Sensitive Scope of Pattern Variables in the** `switch` **Construct**


Analogous to the flow sensitive scope of type patterns in `case` labels (p.


18), the scope of any pattern variable introduced by a record pattern


comprises the `when` clause and the code associated with the `case` label.


**Type Inference of Record Pattern Variables in** `case` **Labels**


Analogous to the type inference of pattern variables with `var` in a record


pattern used in the `instanceof` pattern match operator (p. 23), such type


inference is also performed for pattern variables declared with `var` in


record patterns used in `case` labels. The pattern variables in record


patterns at (1) and (2) above are declared with `var` for type inference of


the pattern variables, where the type of the pattern variables is inferred to be


`int` .


**Case Label Dominance in Record Patterns**


The discussion on case label dominance for type patterns in `case` labels


also applies to record patterns in `case` labels (p. 16). Reversing the order


of the `case` labels (1) and (2) above will result in the unguarded record


pattern to dominate the guarded record pattern, resulting in a compile-time


error.


**Illegal Fall-Through in** `case` **Labels with Record Patterns**


The compiler alerts to any illegal fall-through in an enhanced `switch`


construct with record patterns in `case` labels (p. 19). Fall-through to the


`default` label is allowed in an enhanced `switch` statement that uses the

**Using Generic Record Patterns in** `case` **Labels**


We can specify record patterns for generic record types in the `case` labels


of an enhanced `switch` construct—analogous to record patterns for


generic record types in the `instanceof` pattern match operator (p. 24).


Parameterized record type as reference type of the selector expression


requires `case` labels that make the `switch` construct exhaustive. Below


at (1) is a declaration of a generic record type, `Pair<T>`, whose two


components are of the same type parameter `T` . A record of this type,


parameterized with the type argument `String`, is constructed at (2). The


generic record pattern in (3) is explicitly parameterized with the type


argument `String`, whereas in (4) and (5) the record type is the unbounded


record type `Pair<?>` and the raw record type `Pair`, respectively. The


pattern variable types in (4) and (5) are inferred to be of type `String`


from the record reference `strPair` that is the selector expression. In fact,


any record of type `Pair<T>` will match the record patterns in (4) and (5),


where the types of the pattern variables are inferred from the record type of


the selector expression.


Click here to view code image

```
 record Pair<T>(T item1, T item2) {}

 ...

 Pair<String> strPair = new Pair<>("Milk", "Honey");

 // With parameterization.

 switch(strPair) {

 case Pair<String>(String a1, String a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair1: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

```

```
 // With unbounded wildcard and using var.

 switch(strPair) {

 case Pair<?>(var a1, var a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair2: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 // Without parameterization and using var.

 switch(strPair) {

 case Pair(var a1, var a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair3: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 // Diamond operator:

 switch(strPair) {

 case Pair<>(var a1, var a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair4: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

```

Parameterizing the record type with the diamond ( `<>` ) operator results in a


compile-time error, as shown above at (6), as this operator is not allowed in


this context.


The selector object is compatible with a record pattern if it can be cast to


the record type of the pattern without requiring an unchecked conversion—


meaning that the type safety of the cast is not compromised. Given the


record `intPair` at (1), it is used as the selector object in the enhanced


`switch` construct at (2) and (3). In (2) we see that the type of the selector


expression `intPair` is `Pair<Integer>` that cannot be safely cast to the


type `Pair<String>` of the record pattern—the code will not compile. In


(3) we see that the type `Pair<Integer>` of the selector expression


`intPair` is a subtype of the type `Pair<?>` of the record pattern, but the


record pattern at (3) only covers pairs with the pattern list `(String a1,`


`String a2)` . The `switch` statement is therefore not exhaustive. One


way to make it exhaustive is to use the record pattern in (3a) that will be


matched for all pairs that do not have strings.


Click here to view code image

```
 Pair<Integer> intPair = new Pair<>(100, 100);

 switch(intPair) {

 case Pair<String>(String a1, String a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair5: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 switch(intPair) {

 case Pair<?>(String a1, String a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair6: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 case Pair<?>(var a1, var a2) ->

 System.out.println("Not a Pair of strings.");

 }

```

The code below for matching the raw record at (4) to a parameterized


record pattern at (5) will not compile, as the raw record type `Pair` cannot


be safely cast to the parameterized record type `Pair<String>` of the


record pattern. However, the raw record type `Pair` is a subtype of the


unbounded record type `Pair<?>`, and the pattern list is allowed, but the


`switch` statement is not exhaustive. The record pattern at (7) matches all


pairs whose components are of type `Integer`, as the component types of


the selector object are now compatible with the pattern variables at (7).


However, it is the record pattern at (8) that makes the `switch` statement


exhaustive, as the component types of _any_ selector pair are now compatible


with the pattern variables of type `Object` at (8).


Click here to view code image

```
 Pair rawPair = new Pair(10, 20);

 switch(rawPair) {

 case Pair<String>(String a1, String a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair7: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

 switch(rawPair) {

 case Pair<?>(String a1, String a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair8: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 case Pair<?>(Integer a1, Integer a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair9: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

```

```
 case Pair<?>(Object a1, Object a2) ->

 System.out.println("Pair10: " + a1 + ", " + a2);

 }

```

#### 1.7 Using Qualified Name for Enum Constants in the switch **Construct**


When the type of the selector expression is an enum type, a `switch`


statement specified with enum constants in its `case` labels need not be


exhaustive, regardless of whether it uses the colon ( `:` ) or the arrow ( `->` )


notation. However, a `switch` expression with enum constants in its


`case` labels must always be exhaustive. See also Table 1.2, p. 12.


If the type of the selector expression is an enum type, enum constants can


be specified in the `case` labels without their _qualified name_ —that is


without the name of the enum type. In the `switch` statement and


expression below at (1) and (2), respectively, the enum constants of the


enum type `MachineState` are specified in the `case` labels without the


qualified name of the enum type.


Click here to view code image

```

As the type of the selector expression in the `switch` construct can be of


_any_ reference type, it can be necessary to use the qualified name of the


enum constants, otherwise the compiler will not be able to resolve the name


as an enum constant. In the code below, the enum constants are specified


with their qualified name—otherwise the code will not compile. The


`default` label is necessary, covering all possible values of the selector


type, in order to make the `switch` expression exhaustive.


Click here to view code image

```
 Object obj = MachineState.IDLE; // Supertype referen

 String str1 = switch (obj) {

 case MachineState.IDLE  -> "Doing nothing.";

 case MachineState.BUSY  -> "Too busy.";

 case MachineState.BLOCKED -> "Not available.";

 default          -> "No match found for se

 };

```

In summary, when the type of the selector expression in the `switch`


construct is of an enum type, the names of its enum constants in the `case`


_or_

labels can be qualified unqualified—but if the selector expression is of


any other reference type, the names of enum constants in the `case` labels


_must_ be qualified.


#### **1.8 Unexpected Failure in Pattern Matching**

Even though the `switch` construct may be deemed exhaustive at compile


time, an unexpected failure can occur in pattern matching at runtime when


the value does not match any of the specified patterns. In such cases, the


unchecked `java.lang.MatchException` is thrown to indicate such


failure.


What are known as _separate compilation anomalies_ can result in pattern


matching failure, where the type hierarchy that the patterns reference at


runtime is different from what it was at compile time. For example, this


happens if the set of enum constants of an enum type has changed at


runtime from what it was at compile time, or if the set of permitted subtypes


of a sealed type at runtime has changed from what it was at compile time.


We mention a couple of other cases where such pattern matching failure can


occur. For example, if an accessor method throws an exception when


extracting a component value during matching of a record pattern, pattern


matching completes abruptly and will throw a `MatchException` .

As of Java 21, new interfaces for _sequenced_ types that exhibit an inherent


_well-defined encounter order_ have been integrated into the Java Collections


Framework. These interfaces are seamlessly retrofitted into the existing


type hierarchy to provide a uniform set of operations at both ends, including


a reverse-ordered view. This has been achieved without deprecation of any


existing code in the Java Collections Framework. Introduction of these


sequenced interfaces has resulted in the framework becoming more


versatile and powerful than before.


We assume familiarity with the Collections Framework prior to Java 21,


especially the core interfaces in the `java.util` package.

#### **2.1 Collections with Well-Defined Encounter Order**


A common property of many collections in the Java Collections Framework


is that they have an inherent _well-defined encounter order_ —meaning that


they have a well-defined first element, second element, and so on, right to


the last element. This order imposes a relationship between any two


elements in the collection, where either one element is before or after the


other element. A consequence of this relationship is that the one before is


then closer to the first element and the one after is closer to the last element.


An important implication of the defined encounter order is that, not only


can the elements be processed from the first element to the last element, but


there is a reverse encounter order that allows elements to be processed from


the last element to the first element.


Note that the defined encounter order of a collection does not imply how


the elements are physically stored in memory.


In the past, there has not been a universal collection supertype in the Java


Collections Framework to represent a sequenced collection—that is, a


sequence of elements that has a well-defined encounter order allowing


uniform operations at both ends and offering a reverse-ordered view. The


`List` and `SortedSet` interfaces inherently define an encounter order,


but their common supertype `Collection` is too general and does not


define an encounter order. Similarly the `Set` interface does not define an


encounter order, but its subtypes `SortedSet` and `LinkedHashSet` do.


There was also either no support or inconsistent support for a uniform set of


operations across collections that exhibit a defined encounter order. The


first element of a list can be accessed by the `get(0)` method call, but for a


sorted set, we need to call the `first()` method. Moreover, a deque


provides its own `getFirst()` method for the same purpose. Accessing


the last element is also not consistent: either different methods in each kind


Although all collections provided the `iterator()` method to obtain an


iterator to process elements from the first to the last element in a collection,


there was no standard way to iterate in the reverse direction. One could use


a reverse iterator obtained by calling a specific method in the collection (for


The uniform support for sequenced collections, sets, and maps enhances the


Java Collections Framework, without affecting how the framework was


used previously.

**The** `SequencedCollection<E>` **Interface**


A sequenced collection is a collection whose elements exhibit a defined


encounter order. The behavior of a sequenced collection is dictated by the


`SequencedCollection` interface that provides `default` methods to


_add_, _retrieve_, and _remove_ elements at _both ends_, including a method to


create a _reverse-ordered view_ of such a collection.


Methods to add, retrieve, and remove elements at both ends are _promoted_


from the `Deque` interface that already defined these methods before the


introduction of sequenced collections. Pertinent API details of the methods


in the `SequencedCollection` interface are given below.

`UnsupportedOperationException` in its implementation.


Consider a `List` which has _insertion order_ as its defined encounter order.


Adding, retrieving, and removing elements at either end of a list does not


structurally affect the defined encounter order. The list still remains in


insertion order. However, a `SortedSet` has a _sort order_ as its defined


encounter order that determines by comparison where an element is placed


in the sorted set. Allowing to add an element at either end of a sorted set can


invalidate the sort order, as this might not be the right place for the element


being added according to the sort order.


An _unmodifiable sequenced collection_ does not allow `add*()` and


`remove*()` methods, as that would violate its integrity (p. 62). These


optional methods are thus not allowed on unmodifiable sequenced


collections. Thus, the optional methods of a sequenced collection ensure


that the integrity of its defined encounter order is not compromised.


The _reverse-ordered view_ of the sequenced collection created by the


abstract `reversed()` method is a sequenced collection. Whether changes


in the view are visible in the underlying sequenced collection and vice


versa, is dependent on the implementation of the method provided by the


sequenced collection. Given the reverse-ordered view, it is then possible to


process the elements of a sequenced collection in both directions using any


of the usual iteration mechanisms (for example, an enhanced `for(:)`


loop, an explicit iterator, the `forEach()` method, or iterating using a


stream or an array).

**The** `SequencedSet<E>` **Interface**


The `SequencedSet` interface inherits the behavior of both `Set` and


`SequencedCollection` interfaces, as such a sequenced set can be used


to model both a _set_ that has a defined encounter order or a _sequenced_


_collection_ with no duplicates.


The `SequencedSet` interface inherits the `add*()`, `get*()`, and the


`remove*()` methods for operations at both ends from its superinterface


`SequencedCollection`, and only covariantly overrides the


method to return a .





Click here to view code image

This method is a covariant override of the method from


`SequencedCollection` interface, defined as an `abstract` method,


returning a `SequencedSet` instead of a `SequencedCollection` .


**The** `SortedSet<E>` **Interface**


The `SortedSet` interface provides default implementations of the `add*`


`()`, `get*()`, and `remove*()` methods for operations at both ends by


overriding these methods from its superinterface `SequencedSet`, and


also covariantly overriding the `reversed()` method to return a


`SortedSet` .


The `add*()` methods throw an `UnsupportedOperationException`,


as _explicit positioning_ of elements is not allowed in a sorted set since


elements are positioned by relative comparison to preserve the sort order.


Elements should therefore be added by methods `add()` and `addAll()`


that uphold the sort order.


The implementations of the `get*()` and `remove*()` methods call the


`first()` and `remove()` methods defined by the `SortedSet` interface.

The implementations of the `remove*()` methods call the `poll*()`

#### **2.6 Sequenced Maps**


A map contains _mappings_ (also called _entries_ ) from a set of _key_ objects to a


set of _value_ objects. A key can, at most, be associated with one value—that


is, the key must be unique. Figure 2.2 shows the type hierarchy under the


root interface `Map` that represents all maps in the Java Collections


Framework. The abstract classes that provide the basis on which concrete


.
classes are implemented are not shown in Figure 2.2


Figure 2.2 also shows how the `SequencedMap` interface and its subtypes


that provide support for _sequenced maps_ are retrofitted onto the inheritance


hierarchy of maps. These sequenced interfaces and their sequenced


subtypes (shown colored grey in Figure 2.2) impose an encounter order on


the _entries_ of a sequenced map and define operations on entries at either


end. Maps are _not_ iterable, and further, do _not_ provide an iterator. Iteration


over the entries in a map is normally done indirectly using an iterable


keyset view of the map.

summarized in Table 2.3. Rows colored light grey in Table 2.3 represent


sequenced maps.

**The** `SequencedMap<K, V>` **Interface**


A _sequenced map_ is a map whose _entries_ have a well-defined encounter


order. Its behavior is dictated by the `SequencedMap` interface that defines


methods to add, retrieve, and remove entries at either end of the map. In


addition, it includes a method to create a _reverse-ordered view_ of such a


map, and methods to create three _sequenced views on its keyset, values_


_collection, and entrySet_, respectively.





Click here to view code image

```
 // Optional put methods (promoted from the NavigableM

 default V putFirst(K k, V v)

 default V putLast(K k, V v)

```

The methods insert the specified mapping into the map if it is not present or


they replace the value of the mapping if it is present. In either case, the


specified mapping becomes the first _entry_ or the last _entry_ in this sequenced


map’s encounter order, respectively.


The methods return the value previously associated with `k`, or the `null`


value.


The methods will throw an `UnsupportedOperationException` if the


operation is not supported.


The default implementations of the `put*()` methods in the





Click here to view code image

```
 // Get methods (promoted from the NavigableMap<K, V>

 default Map.Entry<K, V> firstEntry()

 default Map.Entry<K, V> lastEntry()

```

The methods return the first _entry_ or the last _entry_ currently in this


sequenced map, respectively. The methods only retrieve, and do not remove

# **Virtual Threads 3**

Chapter Topics


What virtual threads are and how they compare to platform threads.


How virtual threads are executed.

Creating and using platform threads.


Using executor services to run tasks.








the thread lifecycle, and use different Executor


services and concurrent API to run tasks.



_covered in this_


_chapter._



Introduction of _virtual threads_ promises to facilitate building very high

throughput concurrent applications that employ the one-thread-per-task


paradigm. These lightweight threads are under the regime of the JVM, and


not the operating system. In this chapter we cover what virtual threads are,


explain their high-throughput execution model, create and use them to run


tasks, compare them to platform threads, and provide best practices for


using them. Most importantly, we need hardly learn a new API to utilize


them.


Before going forward, it is highly recommended to have a sound


understanding of the traditional concurrency model based on platform


threads as outlined in the prerequisites at the start of this chapter.

#### **3.1 Motivation for Virtual Threads**


The concurrency model in Java has traditionally centered around _platform_


_threads_ —threads that are scheduled by the operating system and mapped to


_operating system (OS) threads_ in order for them to execute Java code.


Concurrent applications based on _one-thread-per-task paradigm_ strive to


increase their _throughput_ —that is, increase the number of tasks that can be


done concur-rently—by requiring evermore platform threads. However,


constraints on the number of platform threads that can be created and


managed is often the bottleneck when it comes to scalability in concurrent


applications. The constraints can be due to limitations imposed by the


hardware, the operating system, or the sheer size of memory that would be


required to handle vast number of platform threads. One-thread-per-task


style of developing high-throughput concurrent applications with platform


threads therefore becomes infeasible.

#### **3.2 Virtual Thread Execution Model**


:
By design, virtual threads are _lightweight_


They are less expensive to create and destroy than platform threads.


They require substantially less _stack memory_ to manage their execution


than platform threads.


_Context switching_ between virtual threads is far less expensive than


between platform threads.


Virtual threads are managed by the JVM scheduler during their lifetime, as


opposed to platform threads that have a one-to-one mapping with OS


threads and are scheduled by the operating system during their lifetime. In


other words, the whole regime of virtual threads is managed by the JVM


that has a pool of platform threads at its discretion, without the intervention


of the operating system. Because of their nature, virtual threads are ideal for


building concurrent applications based on the one-thread-per-task paradigm,


allowing each task to execute in its own virtual thread.


Execution of virtual threads is illustrated in .
Figure 3.1a As with platform


threads, a virtual thread is first created to run a task and then scheduled to


begin execution. There can be many virtual threads scheduled to begin


execution ((1) in Figure 3.1a). From hereon their execution is at the


discretion of the JVM.


In order to run the task in a virtual thread that is ready for execution, the


JVM scheduler assigns the virtual thread to a _platform thread_ for execution


—this is called _mounting_ the virtual thread ( `vt` ) and the designated


platform thread is called the _carrier thread_ ( `ct` ) ((2) and (5) in Figure 3.1a


showing virtual threads `vt0`, `vt12`, and `vt11` that are mounted on


carrier threads `ct1`, `ct2`, and `ct3`, respectively). A platform thread is


mapped to an OS thread ( `ost` ) and acts as a carrier thread when it is


executing a virtual thread.


**Figure 3.1** _Virtual Thread Execution Model_


Executing certain operations in its task can cause a mounted virtual thread


to _unmount_ from its carrier thread—that it, to relinquish its carrier thread


(as at (2) in Figure 3.1a for virtual threads `vt0` and `vt12` ). A virtual


thread is unmounted when it executes a _blocking operation_ (such as an I/O


operation). It does not require any action on the part of the application to


initiate unmounting when a blocking operation is executed. I/O operations


and other relevant blocking operations in the APIs have been updated to


work with virtual threads. The unmounted virtual thread remains blocked


until its blocking operation is ready to complete ((3) in Figure 3.1a), at


which point, it is unblocked and joins other virtual threads waiting to mount


.
and thus resume execution ((4) in Figure 3.1a)


A virtual thread that completes its execution while mounted is of course


unmounted and terminated ((5) in Figure 3.1a for virtual thread `vt11` ) and


its carrier thread used to mount another virtual thread that is ready to be


mounted for execution.


Instead of a carrier thread being monopolized by its virtual thread until the


blocked operation is ready to complete, unmounting it allows the JVM


scheduler to mount another virtual thread that is ready for execution on the


carrier thread.


An execution profile of a virtual thread is shown in Figure 3.1b, illustrating


that the virtual thread executes when it is mounted on a carrier thread, and


is unmounted and blocked on a blocking operation until the operation is


ready to complete. Note that on resumption of its execution, a virtual thread


may be mounted on the same carrier thread or on a different carrier thread.


The ratio `m:n` of `m` virtual threads to `n` platform threads is usually very


high, contributing to the high-throughput of the virtual thread execution


model. A task assigned to a platform thread remains assigned to the


platform thread throughout its lifetime—even while it is in a waiting or a


blocked state, and cannot therefore do any useful work. The task in a virtual


thread also remains assigned to the same virtual thread through its lifetime,


but the virtual thread may be executed on one or more platform threads,


freeing the carrier thread to do other work when the virtual thread is


unmounted and blocked. The virtual thread execution model results in high


utilization of the platform threads by multitude of virtual threads, which


counts for the high throughput of the one-thread-per-task execution model.


are also known as _classical threads_ or _traditional threads_ .
_Platform threads_


_OS threads_ are also known as _native threads_ or _kernel threads_ .

#### 3.3 Using Thread  Class to Create Virtual Threads


The `Thread` class supports virtual threads and provides new methods for


this purpose. We cannot use a constructor of the `Thread` class to create a


virtual thread as all constructors create platform threads. However, the


Concurrency API provides great flexibility in creating and running virtual


threads, as we will see in the rest of this chapter.


**Logging Information during Program Execution**


Using _blocking_ operations (such as print methods of the `System.out`


stream) to write information about program execution in concurrent


applications can adversely affect program performance. The Logging API


provides a simple, yet flexible _non-blocking_ mechanism to log such


information. There are no direct questions on the exam in this topic, but use


of loggers may be encountered in the context of other questions, such as in


the context of the Concurrency API or execution of parallel streams.


Steps (1)-(4) shown in Example 3.1 are sufficient to create and use a logger


for our purpose, which we will be doing in some examples in this chapter:


1. Import the `Logger` class.


2. Declare a `static` field and create an instance of the `Logger` class.


3. Provide a static initializer block to set property for appropriate format to


be used by the formatter when logging messages. For example:





4. Call the `info()` method of the logger in the program to log messages.

**Creating and Starting a Virtual Thread**


in Example 3.2, passing the task that is to be executed.

 Thread vt = Thread.startVirtualThread(task);

```

A task is defined at (1) as a `Runnable` that prints the _string representation_


of the current thread, which in this case will be a virtual thread, when the


task is executed. Note that the print method is a _blocking_ operation.


Click here to view code image

```
 Runnable task = () -> System.out.println(Thread.curre

```

The virtual method created and started at (2) will execute the task at (1)


when it is allowed to run, printing information about the virtual thread:


Click here to view code image





In this case, the string representation of the current thread comprises of the


following components:


`VirtualThread` identifies that it is a virtual thread.


`#21` specifies the unique _thread ID_ of the virtual thread. In this case it


is `21` . The thread ID does not change during the lifetime of a thread.


`runnable` indicates the _state_ the thread is in. In this case, it is in the


_runnable state_ .


`ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1` is composed of the _name of the fork-_


_join pool_ and the _name of the carrier thread_ on which the virtual thread


is mounted. The name `ForkJoinPool-1` identifies the fork-join pool


that manages the carrier threads (which are platform threads).


Designation `worker-1` is the name of the carrier thread in the fork-join


pool `ForkJoinPool-1` on which the virtual thread with ID `#21` is


mounted.


The number value in the thread ID designation, the carrier thread


designation, and the fork-join pool designation are counter values giving


an indication of how many of these entities have been created.


Virtual threads are daemon threads—that is, they are unceremoniously


terminated when the parent platform thread terminates. The virtual thread


created at (2) in Example 3.2 can risk being terminated before it has


completed if the parent platform thread (in this case, the _main_ thread)


completes first. In order to allow the virtual thread to complete its


execution, the parent thread can call the `join()` method on the virtual


thread in order to wait for its completion before proceeding. The call at (4)


will ensure that the main thread will wait indefinitely and does not proceed


before the virtual thread completes its execution.


Click here to view code image

```
 vt.join();

```

In Example 3.2, the main thread logs information about whether the virtual


thread is alive before and after calling the `join()` method on the virtual


thread. The logged information shows that virtual thread `#21` was alive


before the call to the `join()` method, but had completed its execution


after the call.


Finally, the information logged at (5) in Example 3.2 shows that a virtual


package and not accessible outside this package. For all intents and


purposes, it is the `Thread` class that provides the support for virtual


threads. However, the application has to keep track of whether a reference


of type `Thread` denotes a virtual or a platform thread.

```

A call to this overloaded method invoked on a thread will wait and not


return until either the thread has completed or it is timed out after the


specified duration. It returns `true` if the thread has terminated, `false` if


the thread has not terminated.


It does not wait if the duration to wait is less than or equal to zero. In this


case, it just tests if the thread has terminated.


Click here to view code image

```

```

The current thread sleeps (that is, temporarily ceases execution) for at least


the specified time before it becomes eligible for running again. Note this is


a
_blocking_ operation on the current thread.

**Important Aspects of Virtual Threads**


Example 3.4 shows how virtual threads and platform threads are different in


various aspects. Two unstarted threads, one virtual thread and one platform


thread, are created with names `vt` and `pt` using a virtual and a platform


thread builder, respectively.


**Is a Thread Virtual?**


The `isVirtual()` method of the `Thread` class determines whether a


thread is virtual or not. The output shows that thread `vt` is virtual but


thread `pt` is not. There is no `isPlatform()` method in the `Thread`


class.


**Virtual Threads are Daemon Threads**


The `isDaemon()` method of the `Thread` class determines whether a


thread is daemon or not. The output shows that thread `vt` is daemon but


thread `pt` is not. Trying to set a virtual thread as non-daemon with the


call results in an .
```
setDaemon(false) IllegalArgumentException

```

**Virtual Threads have Normal Priority**


Virtual threads always have `ThreadPriority.NORM_PRIORITY` (=5)


that cannot be changed. Setting a different priority of a virtual thread with


the `setPriority()` method is ignored. The method can readily be used


to change the priority of a platform thread.


**Virtual Threads belong to VirtualThreads Group**


All virtual threads belong to the _VirtualThreads_ group, whereas a platform


thread belongs in a specific thread group. A thread group allows its thread


to be manipulated collectively rather than individually. The output shows


that thread `vt` belongs to the _VirtualThreads_ group, whereas thread `pt`


belongs to the _main_ thread group.

#### **3.5 Using Thread Factory to Create Threads**

A _thread factory_ can be used to create threads on demand. Such a factory


implements the `newThread()` method of the `ThreadFactory` interface


that creates and returns an unstarted thread. A thread factory is _thread-safe_


from multiple concurrent threads, as opposed to a thread builder which is


not.


Thread builders provide the `factory()` method that returns a thread


factory based on the current state of the builder, such as the thread name to


use when creating threads.


Click here to view code image

```
 ThreadFactory vtf = Thread.ofVirtual().name("VT_", 1)

```

In the code above from Example 3.5, the _virtual thread factory_


Unstarted virtual threads are created at (2) by calling the `newThread()`


method of the thread factory and have to be explicitly scheduled to begin


execution by calling the `start()` method of the `Thread` class:


Click here to view code image




Using a platform thread factory obtained from a platform thread builder is


analogous to using a virtual thread factory obtained from a virtual thread


builder.
